sources.title: M. Ahmed, Census of India 1961, Volume XII Part VII-A, Survey of Traditional Crafts, Orissa (published 1967), Book One
sources.inspection: Original PDF extracted and inspected, including imprint PDF6 and preface PDF11–12.
findings: 1962 investigation centred on Penthabahal in then Rairakhol subdivision, Sambalpur district; not a census of all Kamar people. The source explicitly identifies the village smelters as Kamars.

Women helped gather ore, transport charcoal and work the paired foot bellows; the smelting operation depended on coordinated household labour. Furnace was clay; hot iron removed with tongs and worked on a granite anvil.
Practical skill in giving iron useful hardness is described as learned by watching forefathers. Attribute to this report; do not repeat its claim of absence of theoretical knowledge.

Investigators found furnaces operating around Umarkot in February1961 but closed in several villages when revisited in latter1962. Smelters attributed closures to officials stopping removal of ore from reserved forests; this is attributed testimony, not a verified legal finding.
The author also identifies competition from factory iron and difficulty obtaining charcoal. Treat as historical analysis, not current conditions.
Kantilo chapter lists twenty Kamar workers in brass/bell-metal industry, useful optional evidence that identities and occupations do not map one-to-one; would share this same source budget.
limits: Entire publication shares one <=200-word derived-prose budget, including notes. Suggested allocation: ~100 words family work/learning, ~65 change, ~25 source note.
Reject racial appearance/fitness statements, temperament and laziness claims, romantic contentment and universal ancient continuity.
Eleventh-century Kond settlement chronology is unsubstantiated in this inspected account; not community formation evidence.
Distinct Koraput Lohar study must not be silently treated as Kamar identity.
Photographs and captions identify workshop people, but reuse rights not established; no image recommendation.

sources.title: Census of India 1961, village survey Daanla; 1962 investigation, published1968
sources.inspection: Original PDF selected pages extracted and read
findings: Records one Kamar household of seven people; says it arrived in the preceding generation, a local settlement account rather than caste origin.

Separately describes one village blacksmith making axes, sickles, ploughshares and knives and doing repairs. Each draught-animal-owning household paid six seers of paddy annually per pair of bullocks for services.
Villagers shaped wooden handles while metal portions were bought at market or prepared by local blacksmith. This shows interdependent labour rather than a single self-contained craft.
Products surplus to local needs were sold in surrounding villages or Keonjhar market.
limits: One village in the survey period, not present-day universal payment rate.

Household caste count and occupational passage are separate; do not invent a named Kamar artisan or imply every blacksmith was Kamar. Safe wording: the same village study records a Kamar household and describes the blacksmith service.
No inference that preceding-generation household migration gives origin of the community.

findings: Places Badhei, Kamar and Pathuria within its Biswakarma community description, distinguishing wood, iron and stone work.
Specifically associates Kamars with iron implements and household appliances; reports Biswakarma worship.
limits: District account, not an exhaustive Odisha caste map.
Do not universalise its broad intermarriage statement or collapse these named communities into aliases.
Do not infer community identity of every ironworker or every Biswakarma worshipper.
